title: Sunscreen SPF50

drivers.name: Price increase (+4.1%)
drivers.evidence: Two recent weeks at $13.93 saw sales 11% and 16% below baseline; noise-adjusted price effect is x0.97; 4.1% increase likely reduces demand.

drivers.name: Supplier delivery risk
drivers.evidence: Planner notes warn of short delivery; could reduce sellable inventory, lowering actual sales even if demand is stable.

adjustment.analysis: No events or promotions are scheduled. The price increase to $13.93 (+4.1%) is a known demand deterrent. Historical data shows price hikes correlate with demand drops: the last $13.93 week (2026-09-28) sold 27 units (vs baseline 25.2), and the prior one (2026-10-05) sold 21. The noise-adjusted effect of a price increase is x0.97, but with only two data points and no promotion, confidence is low. Supplier delivery risk adds downside uncertainty. No seasonal or event drivers apply. The classical model’s 1.00 is too optimistic. Adjust down for price and supply risk.

brief:
PRODUCT: Sunscreen SPF50 | category Personal Care | Store #12 (Austin, TX)
TARGET WEEK: 2026-10-19 to 2026-10-25 (2 weeks after the last week with sales data)

KNOWN PLAN FOR THE TARGET WEEK:
  events: none
  shelf price: 13.93 (+4.1% vs regular price 13.38)
  planner notes: Supplier warns of a short delivery

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 25.2 | 5%-95%: 2.6 - 55.9 | 10%-90%: 7.2 - 40.3

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-77% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
